@@131952044 <h> G-20 Summit , from Johannesburg to the World : A Blueprint for a Fairer Global Order <h> Share : <p> The G-20 Summit held in Johannesburg marked a defining moment in the global governance landscape . At a time when the world is grappling with soaring geopolitical tensions , rising inequality , and worsening climate shocks , the South African presidency sought to challenge the traditional architecture of power and put forth a new vision of global cooperation . Johannesburg became more than a host city -- it evolved into a symbol of a world demanding fairness , representation , and transformation . This essay critically analyses the summit 's outcomes as a nascent framework for a more equitable global order while simultaneously emphasising the tensions , structural constraints , and political obstacles that persist in influencing international relations . <p> A Lasting Inequality at the Core of Global Governance <p> There is still a lot of inequality in the world , and Johannesburg showed this with clear data . The richest 10% of people in the globe own more than 76% of all the money in the world @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ about 18% of the world 's population but just 3% of its GDP . The ratio is a huge difference that shows how unfair international economic systems are at their core . South Africa used these numbers to say that the way the world is now is not fair or long-lasting . But the G-20 's promise of fairness is constrained because Africa only has one permanent member ( South Africa ) in a group that makes decisions about the economy for 8 billion people . The Johannesburg conference tried to fix the matter by asking for more African representation , especially in the United Nations Security Council ( UNSC ) . Critics , however , highlight that repeated calls for UN reform over three decades have yielded no structural change . The summit 's declarations therefore remain symbolic unless matched by concrete political commitments from major powers . <p> Reimagining the Bretton Woods System : Reform or Rhetoric ? <p> A major theme of the summit was the urgent need to reform global financial institutions -- the IMF , World Bank , and other Bretton Woods organisations . Unsustainable @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Bank , over 60% of low-income countries are either in or at high risk of debt distress , and Africa alone spends $70 billion annually on debt servicing -- more than its spending on healthcare and education combined . South Africa contended that this framework fosters dependency and erodes sovereignty . For example , IMF loans come with policy conditions that generally require cuts to social spending . The Johannesburg summit suggested that concessional finance should be expanded , debt restructuring should be made easier , and unused Special Drawing Rights ( SDRs ) should be moved from rich countries to poor ones . But these ideas show the main problem : the G-20 , which is made up of the countries that control IMF and World Bank voting power , ca n't change global finance on its own without going against strong political interests . The United States has 16.5% of the votes in the IMF , which gives it the capacity to block reforms . In contrast , all of Africa has fewer than 7% of the votes . Calls for fairness do n't mean much unless the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , which is unlikely to happen in today 's world . <p> Climate Justice : The Intersection of Aspiration and Actuality <p> Climate change was key to Johannesburg 's agenda , with South Africa emphasising that the African continent , which accounts for just 4% of total global emissions , endures disproportionate impacts . The UN estimates that climate impacts cost African economies between 3% and 5% of GDP annually . The summit 's declaration urged developed nations to deliver the long-delayed USD 100 billion per year climate finance commitment and scale up to USD 1 trillion annually to support mitigation , adaptation , and resilience . This effort was presented as a cornerstone of a fairer global order . However , critical evaluation shows a gap between ambition and action . Developed countries have repeatedly failed to meet finance pledges ; in 2022 , they provided only $89.6 billion , some of which was repackaged aid or loans instead of grants . Furthermore , climate money is disproportionately allocated -- over 60% is directed towards mitigation , but adaptation , a critical concern for Africa , receives less than @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , particularly South Africa 's $8.5 billion initiative , were presented as exemplars for ecological transition . However , 90% of JETP funds are loans , prompting fears that green development is exacerbating debt dependency . Consequently , whereas Johannesburg bolstered the ethical rationale for climate justice , the financial framework remains profoundly imbalanced . <p> Digital Inequality and the Emerging AI Divide <p> The digital economy was another focal point in the summit 's blueprint for fairness . Africa has the world 's lowest internet penetration rate at 36% , compared to the global average of 67% . Furthermore , the continent generates only 1% of global digital production , while incurring some of the highest data expenses . Johannesburg urged investments in accessible broadband , digital literacy , cybersecurity collaboration , and the establishment of ethical AI standards . The G-20 's emphasis on AI governance is particularly pertinent : as AI becomes integral to economic advancement , emerging nations face the danger of entering a new type of technological reliance . The conference underscored the importance of inclusive AI development ; nevertheless , critics contend that unless @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ companies , located in the US and China , together valued at over $9 trillion -- AI governance frameworks will remain biased . Africa can not achieve technological sovereignty without control over data , computing infrastructure , and skilled human capital . Johannesburg articulated the challenge , but the solutions offered remain aspirational . <p> Food Security and Water Stress : A Growing Crisis <p> Rising global hunger is one of the most alarming challenges discussed at the summit . According to the UN 's 2024 data , well over 735 million individuals suffer from chronic hunger , with Africa representing 282 million -- approximately 40% of the worldwide total . The continent imports more than $50 billion in food each year , despite possessing 60% of the world 's uncultivated arable land . Johannesburg presented initiatives for sustainable agriculture , climate-resilient seeds , and regional food reserves . However , detractors emphasise that these solutions necessitate long-term investment , stable institutions , and technological transfers -- domains in which the G-20 's pledges have traditionally been inadequate . Similarly , water scarcity is worsening . Water scarcity may force @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ by 2030 . South Africa , experiencing persistent droughts , pointed out the urgent need for transboundary water collaboration . The conference featured robust language regarding water security but failed to establish a formal framework , resulting in questionable implementation . <p> It is an ambitious agenda , reflecting the aspirations of a world frustrated by inequality and broken promises . The summit reinforced the Global South 's rising diplomatic confidence -- building on the momentum of Indonesia ( 2022 ) , India ( 2023 ) , and Brazil ( 2024 ) . But the blueprint also has boundaries . ( a ) The G-20 is not a treaty organisation ; its decisions are non-binding. ( b ) Structural reforms require political will from major powers unwilling to reduce their influence . ( c ) Climate finance , digital access , and global health continue to suffer from chronic underfunding . Lastly , geopolitical tensions threaten collective action and fragment global priorities . Consequently , Johannesburg 's framework serves as a potent moral compass yet is limited as a catalyst for transformation . <p> Conclusion : Johannesburg 's Promise and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Johannesburg , conveyed a pressing demand for equity , representation , and justice on a global scale . It contested the inequitable foundations of the global order with persuasive facts and principled arguments . Nevertheless , the persistent inquiry endures : Can a forum influenced by the world 's most dominant nations truly reform the system that serves their interests ? The Johannesburg summit delineates the framework ; yet , the pursuit of a more equitable global order necessitates structural reforms , political fortitude , and an authentic dedication to global solidarity . The world 's adherence to this framework is questionable ; yet , the ethical and strategic imperative for change has never been more evident . <h> Subscribe to Our Newsletter <p> Dr Syed Mohammad Raghib is a scholar affiliated with Jawaharlal Nehru University ( JNU ) , where he has been involved with the School of International Studies . @@131960678 <h> walrus haulout Photograph : ( WWF-Russia ) <p> Story highlights <p> According to Rod Downie from WWF , walruses play a key role in keeping the Arctic ecosystem healthy , and their decline can affect many other species . <p> Scientists have made an important new discovery in the Arctic after finding a surprising group of walruses ( a large animal that lives in or near the sea in Arctic regions ) on the remote shores of Svalbard , a region located between mainland Norway and the North Pole . This discovery was possible through the Walrus from Space project , run by the World Wide Fund for Nature ( WWF ) and the British Antarctic Survey ( BAS ) . <p> The newly identified walrus haul-out in Svalbard is a major step forward for Arctic research . A haul-out is a place where many walruses gather on land and this one had never been recorded before . <p> It was spotted using satellite photos as part of the Walrus from Space program . Since 2021 , thousands of volunteers have helped to search these images to find and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> This project has become more important because walruses are under growing pressure from climate change . These huge animals , which can weigh up to two tonnes , depend on sea ice to rest . As the ice melts earlier and returns later each year , walruses struggle to find safe places to gather . <p> According to Rod Downie from WWF , walruses play a key role in keeping the Arctic ecosystem healthy , and their decline can affect many other species . <h> The growing need for Walrus protection <p> As the climate warms , twice as fast in the Arctic as in the rest of the world , walruses face serious threats from shrinking sea ice , human activity and environmental damage . <p> WWF and BAS are not only studying walruses but also pushing for stronger climate policies . Information from the Walrus from Space project is helping scientists to better understand the challenges these animals face and plan better ways to protect them in the neat future .
